summary: Tenzing-Hillary Airport, named after the first two confirmed summiteers of Mount Everest, serves as the primary gateway to the Khumbu region and the trailhead for most Everest treks. Perched at roughly 2,845 meters (9,334 ft) in the Himalayas, it is renowned worldwide for its exceptionally short, sloped runway and dramatic cliff-edge approach. The airport is a vital lifeline for the region's tourism, trekking, and Sherpa communities.
faqs:
Q: Why is Lukla Airport considered one of the most challenging airports in the world?
A: Its runway is only about 527 meters (1,729 ft) long, slopes upward at roughly 12%, and ends directly at a steep drop-off into the valley. There is no radar or instrument landing system, so pilots must rely on visual flight rules and the weather must be clear to land.

Q: Can I fly to Lukla year-round?
A: Scheduled flights operate throughout the year but are highly weather-dependent. The peak trekking seasons of spring (March–May) and autumn (October–November) have the most reliable flying conditions, while monsoon season (June–August) and winter often bring delays or cancellations.

Q: Which airlines operate at Tenzing-Hillary Airport?
A: The main carriers are Tara Air, Yeti Airlines, and Sita Air, offering flights to and from Kathmandu and sometimes Manthali (Ramechhap). Flights use small twin-engine turboprop aircraft such as the DHC-6 Twin Otter.

Q: Do I need a permit to fly into Lukla?
A: A flight ticket alone is enough to board, but trekkers continuing into the Everest region typically need a TIMS card and the Sagarmatha National Park entry permit, which can be arranged in Kathmandu or at Monjo.
transport_tips: Most travelers reach Lukla via a 30–45 minute flight from Kathmandu, often routed through Ramechhap (Manthali) Airport during peak seasons to ease congestion in Kathmandu. Arrive early for your flight as boarding procedures are informal and delays are common due to mountain weather. There are no road connections to Lukla, so flying is the only practical option for entering or leaving the town.
